utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth and the interpreters; good morning to the staff of the Registry, the Prosecution and the Defence. Today we're going to continue our video-conferences, and I think the next witness is Drasko Dzervida. Is that right, Mr. Jovan Simic? MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] That's right, Mr. President, and the cross-examination [sic] will be conducted by Mr. Masic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that we have lost our communication line with the witness. It's back. Good morning, Drasko Dzervida. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please stand. Thank you. You're now going to read the solemn declaration handed to you. Please go ahead. Read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me start off by thanking you for coming, Witness, and for cooperating with us. For the moment, you're going to be answering questions put to you by Mr. Masic. Mr. Masic, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dzervida?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Can you hear me properly?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: I can hear you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: For the record, would you give us your full name and surname, your father's name, and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: My name is Drasko Dzervida, born on the 15th of November, 1971. The name of my father is Slobodan, and my mother's name is Milana.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Where do you reside now?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: I reside in Gradina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Do you know Dragoljub Prcac?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes, I know Dragoljub Prcac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: How long have you known him and how come -- how did you come to know him?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: I have known Dragoljub Prcac because my father is the same generation. They're the same age. So I used to see him when I was a child, and I remembered him as a very fine and honest man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: In 1992 were you mobilised, and if so, into what unit?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes. In 1992 I was mobilised in the 143rd Prijedor Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Were you in the investigation centre of Omarska, and if so, in what capacity?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes, I was in the Omarska Investigation Centre as a worker in the kitchen; that is to say, I assisted in the preparation of food.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Was that the task of your unit?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: It was my task because I'm a waiter by profession. So I was used to doing work of that kind and could assist the people in the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: When were you taken prisoner by the Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: I was taken prisoner on the 12th of September, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: How long did you spend in captivity and where were you held?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: For approximately nine months I was in Buzim Bihac at Zazine, in the barracks there, and in the investigation in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: When were you exchanged?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: On the 8th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: What was their conduct to you when you were in prison and what were the kinds of conditions you had during your captivity?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: As far as the conditions and their attitude, I can say that I'm very sorry that I had to live through all of that and experience it all, and the conditions that myself as a human being had to contend with there, although I was a soldier, were barely bearable. As a member of the Republika Srpska army, I was taken prisoner, but the torture that I lived through there is a very difficult experience, and I'm sorry to have experienced it as a human being, to have to go through all of them. They were terrible problems and I can't even begin to explain them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: In the prison, did you make any statements and, if so, under what conditions did you make those statements?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes. While I was in prison, I did give statements. They were given after several days of beating, under duress, under forced labour, and the statements that I made were preceded by psychological and physical abuse and beatings. And afterwards, after all that, I had to sign a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Did you read what you signed, the statement you signed?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: For the most part, the statements that I signed I did not read.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: The facts that you presented in those statements, did you ever tell anybody in the prison about them ever?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dzervida. I have no further questions for you. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Masic. The Prosecution. Yes, I see Mr. Deretic on his feet. You wanted to ask a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just two short questions for this witness with your indulgence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Can you hear me, Mr. Dzervida?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in addition to yourself, were there other Serbian prisoners held captive there?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes, there were other Serbian prisoners held captive.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: And one more question: Do you happen to know whether they gave statements in the same way you did, the so-called statements?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Well, the so-called statements were given by all of them under duress. They had to give them and had to write them regardless of the conditions, that is, they were forced.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, witness. Thank you Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Thank you, Mr. Deretic. I don't see any other Defence counsel getting up. Now it's the Prosecution's turn, and Mr. Saxon, I believe. Witness, you are now going to be answering questions put to you by the Prosecutor. Please proceed, Mr. Saxon. Your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I begin, I have to note that the direct examination and Mr. Deretic's questions took a total of about six minutes. I have prepared a fairly short cross-examination today, but I honestly cannot say that I could finish my cross-examination in six minutes. I would simply ask that the Trial Chamber give me some latitude this morning with respect to the ordinary rule regarding length of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you have it, Mr. Saxon. As always, we are flexible. We have to have rules, but rules -- there are exceptions to every rule so please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I would like that Prosecution Exhibit 3/262 be distributed, and if a B/C/S version of this exhibit could be placed on the ELMO, please, so that the witness can see it in Banja Luka. For the interpreters for their convenience, this is a document the English version has at the top of it International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. It has ERN number 01901957 at the top, and there is also a B/C/S version. If Mr. Usher, if you could place the first page of that B/C/S version on the ELMO, please, so that the witness can see it. Mr. Usher, could you turn that to the last page, please, where there is a signature, or hopefully there will be a signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Dzervida, can you see that page on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can the registrar in Banja Luka assist me. Is it that the monitor is not functioning or is simply the page is not visible?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The AV section has just informed me that it will take a few seconds to coordinate it in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: While we're waiting, Mr. Dzervida, do you recall giving a statement to Defence counsel Jovan Simic a few weeks ago on the 3rd of April?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you recall signing that statement as well?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you look at the screen in front of you. I'm wondering if there is the last page of your statement visible to you now; can you see it?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: I'm very sorry but no, I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to try to move forward without you actually looking at the statement you gave. I'm going to read you a portion of it and see if you will -- can at least comment on it and hopefully agree to it. I have an English version of the statement that you gave in my hand, and I'd like to read the second paragraph of your statement out loud, please. The second paragraph of your statement reads: "Throughout the duration of the Omarska Investigation Centre, I worked preparing food for the army and detainees at the separation," which I think refers to the Separacija building, "which was at the very entrance into the camp. I mostly sliced bread and only went to the centre of the mine, that is, to the administration building, a couple of times." Do you recall telling that to Mr. Jovan Simic on the 3rd of April?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And is that still your testimony today, what I just read to you?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In May of 1992, were you in good physical condition?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did we get an answer?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: The line was disconnected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you hear me now, Mr. Dzervida?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: I can hear you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In May of 1992, were you in good physical condition?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes, I was in good physical condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Usher, if you could assist me. If you could turn that statement to the first page so the witness will at least be able to see what I've read to him. The first page of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Dzervida, can you see that page on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you see that second paragraph that I read out to you a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So just to understand you, to understand your testimony, during May, part of May, June, July, and part of August of 1992, you worked in the Separacija, in the kitchen; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And primarily what you did was slice bread, right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes. Mostly I sliced bread and helped with the loading and unloading.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you part of a quartermaster unit that worked in that kitchen?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We'll come back to that in a minute. If you recall, when was your first day working in that kitchen in the Separacija?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly after everything I lived through, but I do know that it was sometime at the end of May, beginning of June. End of May, beginning of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall when the detention centre at Omarska opened, when the first detainees were brought there?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: I can't say exactly, but the beginning of June thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In your statement, you mentioned that you went to the administration building a couple of times, in the statement that you gave to Jovan Simic. Is that still your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes, it's still my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What did you see when you got to the part of the mine where people were being detained?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Generally during that period when I went down there taking food, the people who were down there in the investigation centre were having their meal and were standing in line to go to lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You're talking about the people who were detained there? They were standing in line?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes. They were waiting to have their meal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you talk to any guards or prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How did the prisoners look when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Well, as it was summer, the detainees did not look frightened in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. They didn't look frightened. How did they look?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The interpreter apologises. The witness said, "They looked tired and frightened."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where in the Omarska camp or investigation centre did you go?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Could you explain what you mean where did I go?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you enter any buildings or did you remain outside?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: No. I didn't go into any building, just twice when I unloaded the food and then I went back to the main kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The main kitchen in the Separacija; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: The main kitchen was at the entrance to the mine itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that was in the Separacija building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "Separacija"? The main administration building. Actually, the main kitchen was at the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Was that close to the Separacija?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: No, it's not near the Separacija.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, in your statement given to Jovan Simic, you said: "I worked preparing food for the army and detainees at the separation." What was the "separation"?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Let me explain. Separacija-- the whole mine is known as Separacija. Where I myself was preparing the food is at the very entrance, a building at the very entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that's where you and the other members of the quartermaster were working?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of the head of that quartermaster unit working in that kitchen during the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes. It was Pero Rendic. He was in charge of the food preparation and setting the norms and standards for the meals.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did that quartermaster unit that you were working in have to work very hard in order to prepare meals for thousands of people every day?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that it really was very strenuous working to prepare the food.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How many soldiers were assigned then to work in that unit in the kitchen with you during May, June, July, and August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: I can't tell you the exact number, but not too many because there were some women there who had been there before the war. They worked in the mine before the war and so worked there to help out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you give us an estimate, please? You were there, the bread slicer; how many other soldiers were there?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact number, but there might have been at most, ten soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At most, ten soldiers.

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: But there were the women there too. The ones that worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Dzervida, Mr. Pero Rendic testified in this courtroom a few months ago. And he talked about his role as the Commander of the quartermaster unit in the kitchen during the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And for the benefit of the Chamber and counsel, I'm looking at page 7321. And Mr. Rendic was asked, "Can you explain the composition of the personnel involved in food preparation?" Mr. Rendic responded, "I have already said that once I had met the mine personnel, I realised that they would not be able to accomplish the tasks assigned to us. I looked for a man who would be a professional cook, also a professional butcher so that together with me, because I was the one organising these activities, to be able to carry out the tasks assigned to us." Then Mr. Rendic was asked, "In addition to you, a butcher, and a cook, were there other army members in this squad involved in food preparation?" Mr. Rendic answered, "No. No one else. The rest were just women workers, the cooks in the iron ore mine, who were under obligation." How can you explain the contradiction between your testimony today and Mr. Rendic's testimony of a few months ago before this Trial Chamber that there was just himself and two other men working in that kitchen during the summer of 1992 and no mention of any man assigned to slice bread. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: All I know is that I worked there, that I sliced bread, and that I helped with the loading and unloading of the food. Perhaps Mr. Pero Rendic didn't remember correctly because so much time has passed, nine years. Perhaps he forgot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Pero Rendic did remember about the unloading of the food and the transportation of the food. I'll tell you what he said about that. Mr. Rendic, he was asked, "The soldiers or rather the individuals Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 who distributed the food, were they members of the units you, yourself, belonged to but not your sector; is that right?" This is on page 7331 of the transcript. Answer: "No, they were quite different soldiers. These were soldiers whose sole task it was to dispatch the food as ordered by the assistant logistics commander." So Mr. Rendic said that the men who worked for him in the kitchen were not involved in dispatching food. The truth is, Mr. Dzervida, you were a guard in the Omarska camp during 1992, were you not? I have not heard a response. Can you hear me, Mr. Dzervida?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: I can hear you now, but I didn't hear you a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you hear my question? My question was --

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The truth is that you were a guard in the Omarska camp during 1992; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: No, gentlemen, I apologise. Perhaps there was a mistake. I was not. I was in the mine slicing bread and preparing the food, I mean helping to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How long did the Omarska camp last, when did it close down?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: I can't say exactly. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: I can't say exactly how many days, but it might have been about two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: One more question: In your statement to Mr. Jovan Simic a few weeks ago, you said that you were mobilised as a soldier of the Republika Srpska at the beginning of the war on the 25th of May 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes. About the 20th or 25th of May. I can't give you an exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you recall when there was an incident in the village of Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: I don't remember that, but I did hear that there was an incident in Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't like to object, but this is lasting five times longer than the examination-in-chief, this cross-examination. I do apologise. And I did not mention Hambarine at all, nor did I ask anything about Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to tell you something, Mr. Masic. Now, with respect to the time, yesterday, you said that you would be taking half an hour. You said that there was a statement and we have the statement before us. And so we must -- the Prosecutor has prepared for at least half an hour and I have that under my control. The other matter is that in this particular declaration, I see the mention of Hambarine. Therefore, I overrule your objection and I think that Mr. Saxon has already said that this is his last question, but I am expecting half an hour, because that is what you implied yesterday. Mr. Saxon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I will try to complete this and tighten it up at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In the first paragraph of the statement that you gave on the 3rd of April, you said, "Investigation centres in Omarska and Keraterm were established after the incident in the village of Hambarine, the blocking of an army convoy in Kozarac, and the attack on Prijedor town." My question for you then is: What were the dates of these events, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Generally towards the end of May and beginning of June. I really can't give you any exact dates. And I have sworn that I would tell the truth so the end of May, beginning of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever see Dragoljub Prcac in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: In the Omarska camp, I saw Dragoljub Prcac maybe once or twice in the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Mr. Masic, you have the opportunity to re-examine the witness so you can respond to the questions asked by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. The Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Deretic, what about you? Any re-examination on your part?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Judge Fouad Riad has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dzervida. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just -- I would like to understand a little bit more your itinerary as a soldier in the Republika Srpska army. You were mobilised, as you said, on the 25th of May, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Approximately. I can't remember the exact day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And immediately you went to Omarska Investigation Centre?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you had nothing else to do there but to cut bread, as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Generally I cut bread and helped with the loading and unloading. Generally that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: After that, what did you do after you left Omarska? Did you participate -- how did you become a prisoner? How were you taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: As a member of the Army of Republika Srpska, as I had been mobilised, I was taken prisoner at Buzim near Bihac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And did you continue working in kitchens or did you participate in other activities?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: No, I didn't take part in any activities for the most part. I was mostly in the kitchens, depending on the need. I didn't take any part in any action. I was linked to the rear, the logistics platoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you were taken prisoner as a cook?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: As a cook, I -- just a moment, please. I can't quite hear. In the -- in the locality I was taken prisoner, I was not taken prisoner as a cook. We were there guarding the line, defending the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you participated in fighting? You were a soldier?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: I was a soldier, but I did not take part in the fighting. I was a soldier, but I did not take part in the fighting because I was not bodily able for that. So I didn't take part in any combat, until that day when the attack took place and when I was taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You were not bodily able and you still were mobilised. Did they mobilise unable people?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: How do you mean "bodily able"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Usually did they mobilise healthy young men or did they mobilise anybody?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Well, generally just healthy people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Thank you too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Judge Fouad Riad. Madam Judge Wald has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Dzervida, I only have one question. When you saw Mr. Prcac once or twice in the kitchen when you were in the Omarska camp, what was your impression that his job was in the Omarska camp? What did you think his job was when you saw him there in the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: At that time, in view of the fact that I was young, I was only 20, about 20, I couldn't assess that, but as I knew Dragoljub from before, I knew he was a good and fine and honest man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Can you tell us perhaps what he was doing in the kitchen when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: Well, generally he was just passing by. He wasn't doing anything special.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Was it your impression that he was a guard or something else?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: I really can't say from my experience. As I say, I was really young and I don't know what function he had. And as I say, I pledged to tell the truth, so I really don't know. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Wald. Witness Dzervida, I, too, am going to ask you some questions following on from that question. Your father or other people, did they tell you what Mr. Prcac was doing in the camp, why he was there?

utterances.speaker: DRASKO DZERVIDA
utterances.text: No, nobody told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Very well. We have no further questions for you, Witness Dzervida. We thank you very much for having come to cooperate with us, and we wish you a safe journey back to your house. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Very well. Mr. Deretic, can we hear another witness now? Perhaps we could have another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, but if you could give us half a second to change places. It's a little uncomfortable for me to ask questions from this position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. Yes, of course you can change places. Right. I see we already have the witness. You can look at the monitor. This is Witness [redacted].

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Mr. President. However, yesterday we had some trouble regarding a pseudonym, and I should like to ask the technical service, because I believe we asked for the protective measures for this witness. So will the technical service help us in relation to this matter? I'm afraid that yesterday there was a switch between these two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me? What are you -- what do you mean that there was a switch, a permutation?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was mention of the protection of the first witness we heard yesterday, although the protective measures -- those protective measures were not asked for that witness, and I believe that the protective measures asked were applied on behalf of this witness. That is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. So what you are telling us is that there may be some questions which you wish to ask in a private session. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite so, but we also asked for full protection for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the question -- it is somewhat difficult to understand the language that you're using. What does it mean "full protection"? I believe we have already discussed this before and agreed that we should have in a way a mixed session because there are certain questions which can't be asked in open session. Then there are also may be questions which can be asked in a private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since you mentioned the full name of the witness, the Defence will not insist on this. We already talked of this witness, but we shall resort to our rights according to the Rules, and when we decide that we need to go into private session because we shall have to mention some of the names which have been arising during this trial, then we shall ask you to do so, that is, to go into private session. So I believe we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is, of course, possible to grant a pseudonym, that is to delete from the transcript the name of the witness which I had already uttered. Of course the witness can be given a pseudonym, and in case of some questions and answers, you can apply for a private session. Would that be all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, definitely so, Mr. President. I thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does the Prosecutor have any objections to this? Excuse me, I do not know, I'd like to know before we begin with the examination who will cross-examine the witness, because I need to know who I am talking to. So who will be cross-examining the witness. Very well. Ms. Susan Somers, do you have any objections to -- against these protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, the Chamber had given us an opportunity last week to voice our objections which we did. If I recall correctly, we did put the ultimate measures in your hands, in the Chamber's hands. We think it highly unreasonable on the part of the Defence to seek protective measures, at least a pseudonym and the other measures. We fully support the Chamber's wise suggestion of going into closed session as appropriate or private session as appropriate, and I think when I have a chance to cross-examine, the Chamber will see that there is really no basis for this request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber will confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber will grant a pseudonym to this witness and will ask the Defence counsel to work in open court. However, when you need to go into a private session, you will tell us so and we have already discussed this. You should organise your examination-in-chief so as to ask if possible in an open session, and then to put together the questions that you will be asking in a private session. I believe that the pseudonym granted this witness will be DD/9. Right. Let us begin. Good morning, Witness DD/9, can you hear me? I am addressing you that way because -- as a result of the decision that was taken here. Can you hear me therefore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you stand, please. You will now read the solemn declaration which the young lady who is standing by you will hand over to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You may be seated. Thank you very much, Witness DD/9. Thank you for coming. Now you will answer questions that Mr. Deretic will ask you. Mr. Deretic, the witness is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with your leave, I should like to ask you to go into private session while we go through the particulars for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Let us move into private session, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You can -- yes. We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness DD/9, were you assigned to the duty of a guard in that investigation centre?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And when did you begin to work as a guard in that investigation centre?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Well, the 4th of June. I think that was my first shift there.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And what was your duty as a guard in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: To be a guard, to stand guard. To stand guard and provide security in that investigation centre.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you tell us who assigned you to that post?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you tell us who assigned you to that guard post?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes. We were all assigned there by Zivko Knezevic, the then Commander of the police station in Prijedor. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was he your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Although you already told us that, but I will ask you once again: Which duties did Zivko Knezevic perform at that time?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Zivko Knezevic was the Commander of the -- or the chief of the police station Prijedor 2.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Where was this police station?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: This police station was at Urije.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did the Keraterm Investigation -- was the Keraterm Investigation Centre at a place which was under the jurisdiction of this police station?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness DD/9, can you tell us, to which guard post were you assigned?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: I was assigned to -- to the left of the scales of the weigh hut. There was a bunker with a machine-gun. I mean there was a barricade with a machine-gun. So there and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You said there was a barrier. What was it made of?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Sandbags. Just ordinary bags filled with sand. And there was a machine-gun on them, and it was covered with canvas, something like that, you known, tarpaulin.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And what machine-gun was it?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: It was an old machine-gun. I think it was -- M-53 is its proper name.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And after you came to that investigation centre, do you remember if there were any persons detained there?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you remember how many rooms there were with persons detained in them at that time?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. There were two such rooms.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know what numbers were attached to them?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Number 1 and number 2.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And after your assignment there, was there yet another room that was in use at that time at the investigation centre?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe one of those days or perhaps a little later, they -- before and after, there was another room for Serb soldiers. What do you call them? Reservists or whatever. Something like detention units. Something like a prison.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So in addition to the guard post where you were, which you described to us, was there at the time perhaps another machine-gun nest?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: No, not then.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And later?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes, there was one later.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Will you tell us when was it set up and what did it look like?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you exactly. Perhaps a few days later, another barrier with sandbags was made and another old machine-gun was placed there.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Where was it?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: To the right of the scales of the weigh hut, weigh bridge.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, as you enter the main gate of the Keraterm Investigation Centre, where was it in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: As you enter the investigation centre, to the right to the weigh bridge.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness, and how long did you perform this duty at the investigation centre in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. If I arrived there sometime around the 4th, then I was there until about the 14th of the same month. Until the middle of that month, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And how did you leave the investigation centre?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We could not understand the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: I was driven away. Zivko Knezevic drove me away because I was avoiding to be there; that is, I was there, but I would often absent myself, go home or to pubs, and I wasn't -- I wasn't up to his -- I wasn't really complying with his rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness, did you know Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When did you come to know him?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Well, since childhood, because we were neighbours.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How far is your flat from the Zigics' family house?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Well, some 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were you friends when you were children, were you friends with Zoran?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And did you remain friends until the war and during the war?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Well, we did not socialise regularly, but we were still friends.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Are you -- did you know that Zoran Zigic played an instrument?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes, he was a musician. He played, yes. People knew him that way.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And after you arrived at the investigation centre at Keraterm, did you find Zoran there?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: We came there together.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was Zoran wounded at about that time?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes, he was wounded.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know which part of the body?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: He was wounded or rather his finger on the -- his left hand, his index finger of the left hand was cut, torn off.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And do you know where Zoran Zigic worked before the war?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes, I know. He was a taxi driver in Prijedor. And after that, he left with his family to Pula. That is where he lived right up until the war.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And after you arrived in Keraterm together, do you know what Zoran's duty was?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Same as mine. Just a plain guard.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: But did he have any special assignment?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you ever see him drive a mini bus, a van?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What kind of a vehicle was it?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Well, it was a light blue and white.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know why did he drive that mini bus?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Well, he brought in food, water, took us back home, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And was that the chief duty of -- Zoran Zigic's chief duty while he was in Keraterm, in fact?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes, the only one. Yes, I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you tell us when did Zoran Zigic perform this duty, was it in daytime or at night?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: In daytime, he would bring food and water, sometimes he would do it in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And did you ever see Zoran Zigic come to Keraterm at night?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: A while ago, you mentioned that Zoran Zigic had been wounded. Was his left hand bandaged?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes, it was bandaged and it hurt him terribly.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did he complain to you about the pain?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes, he did. Yes, he complained. He was saying that he was in much pain.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: During your duty, when you were on duty in daytime, did you used to see Zoran Zigic every day?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You said that you knew him since your childhood days. Did you ever -- since you were children until your departure from the Keraterm Investigation Centre, did you ever see Zoran Zigic with dyed hair?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: No, he is dark haired.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you ever see him wear an earring at that time?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: No, he was always against it.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you ever see him wear black gloves on his hands?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know until when did Zoran keep this bandage on his left hand?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: He had it for a long time, I think for about two or two and a half months, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness, do you know somebody called Said Jusufagic called Car?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: He was a Muslim from Prijedor, a notorious criminal from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know if Car was brought to the investigation at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes, he was brought there.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know when?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: The first day, the first day when we came on duty in Keraterm, there were already people who were there for us, the territorial ones. And in the afternoon hours, that is, after mid-day is when he was brought in.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you see him being brought to the -- into the investigation centre?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What was he brought in?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: He was brought in a police car, we called them Black Marias.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And at the time of detention, did Car have anything with him?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes. He was brought in with a machine-gun, with an older machine-gun, you called them, what do you call them, M-53.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you describe him in just one sentence, what did he look like?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Thin, small, fair haired with a tooth missing or teeth missing.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And when Car was brought in this Black Maria, where were you?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: I was on my guard post to the left of the weigh bridge in front -- by the barrier, sandbag barrier.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: After he was taken out of the Black Maria, do you remember what happened next?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, briefly. Describe what happened as far as you can remember.

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Some ten soldiers jumped on him and pulled him out of the police van and started beating him. They took out a machine-gun. It was empty, without any ammunition. And then Zigic came up and said, "Put the machine-gun on your soldier and run round in a circle. That's what you get for shooting at Serb soldiers and policemen. And now you're going to carry the machine-gun and start running in a circle," and that's what he did. He started running in a circle, and the people who were there started beating him with different objects, with their fists, with their rifles.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you see whether Zigic -- whether Zoran Zigic, in addition to ordering him to put the machine-gun on his shoulder, whether he hit him?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Possibly he did, but I don't remember. It is possible that he hit him once or twice, but I can't say for sure. I don't remember, because there were a lot of soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you remember how long this running around lasted?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: It lasted a long time, perhaps half an hour. I can't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you see Zoran Zigic on that occasion? Was he there?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Zoran Zigic stayed there for a short time. He didn't stay there for long, perhaps 15 minutes, and then he got on his motorcycle and went off, probably to have a drink somewhere.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: After Zigic left the Keraterm compound, was Car still running round in circles?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: After that running, do you know what happened to Car?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: He was removed to Room 2.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know after this occurrence whether Car was beaten at all?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes, I do know.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know somebody by the name of Zoran Karlica?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes, I do know somebody by that name.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: He was a major of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did he take part in the defence of the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes, he did take part in the defence of Prijedor, which is when he was wounded. He was seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know who wounded him?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: It was rumoured that it was Hadzija and his band, his group.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you personally know that man Hadzija?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I knew him from town.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know when Karlica was buried?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes, I do. He is buried on the 6th of June.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: After the funeral, do you know what happened in the Keraterm compound?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to tell us briefly what happened.

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Well, it was roughly like this: I can't say exactly to the hour and half hour, but I know that soldiers turned up around 4.00, perhaps 5.00, perhaps it was 4.30, I'm not quite sure, but a lot of the soldiers came back from the funeral, and there were quite a few funerals in Prijedor during those days. Mika came up, and they called him mitraljezac Car. Car was called the Machine-gunist. That's what they called him. They brought him out, then they trod on him, beat him. There were quite a lot of soldiers there. I can't say exactly how many, but they would come in groups of five, of ten, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you watch this beating?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes, I watched it for a time, for about an hour, because it went on from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Where did this take place?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: It took place in front of Rooms 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: After this happened, do you know whether Car was sent back to the room he was taken out of?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: No, he wasn't taken back. The soldiers didn't let him be taken back to the room. Two men stood guard by him and he just lay there. He was moaning, but you could see that he was going to succumb.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: That evening, were you yourself on duty?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes, I was on duty that evening.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did Car succumb to the beatings?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes, he did. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When did you learn about that?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: I learnt about it in the morning, because we didn't go up to him. We didn't approach him.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When he was beaten was Zoran Zigic present?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you ever see, after this event with Car running around, did you ever see Zoran beat anybody?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When this man was beaten, was Zoran Zigic in the Keraterm Investigation Centre compound at all?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness, during the time you spent in the Keraterm Investigation Centre, did you hear of somebody called Emsud Bahonjic?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes, I did, on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you happen to know whether that individual was beaten up in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you know whether the man had a nickname of any kind after he arrived in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness, did you know from Prijedor somebody called Edin Ganic?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes, I did know him.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you know his father?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What was his father's name?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: His father's name was Huse Ganic. His sister was Edina Ganic.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Where did they live?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: In the upper Muslim part.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Is that a neighbourhood of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes, it's a neighbourhood of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: During your stay in Keraterm, did you ever see Edin Ganic and Huse in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You said that you were -- went away from Keraterm together with Zoran Zigic, that you were dismissed. Do you know whether Zoran Zigic could have taken part in any way in the beating up of these two men?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: No. No. There was no possibility of that. It was absolutely impossible. The people weren't in Keraterm while we were there.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know whether Edin Ganic had any -- had had any problems with the law in Prijedor and generally speaking with the law in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is irrelevant, and has nothing to do with his being beaten in Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did you say was not relevant? I didn't quite follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Any brushes, Your Honour, which Edin Ganic may or may not have had with the law in Prijedor have no bearing on his status in terms of being beaten in Keraterm camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's see. Mr. Deretic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm not quite clear what is meant by this objection. I could ask Mr. Fila here who was the oldest of us whether he was in Keraterm, whether he was beaten up there. I have a reason for asking that. I have my reasons, and Madam Prosecutor must show a little patience and see what I'm leading up to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Deretic, go ahead with your question and we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, after this question, and the answer by the witness, I wanted to call upon the usher, although I did propose earlier on that a document be shown here and be admitted into evidence; however, that has not been done to the present date. So I am tendering it once again, and would the usher come up and hand you the original of the document. I would like him to distribute the document to the Prosecution and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will just wait one second and then I will respond. May the Prosecution also have a copy, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Prosecution and for the Defence as well, please. With your permission, Mr. President, before my learned colleague takes the floor. Mr. President, I have given you the original of the document that I asked from the security service centre from the criminal records for individuals who were mentioned here today, and I should like to tender the document into evidence as showing that the individuals that I mentioned do have a criminal record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I repeat my objection on the ground of relevance. Furthermore, the witness said he did not know about any criminal record and, therefore, to hammer this into the witness is nothing but leading a witness when he has indicated he does not know. Thirdly, the document that has been handed to the Chamber and for our view as well is a summary. It is a letter prepared for litigation. It is not an official archived document and, therefore, there's no way to check whether or not any of the contents is possibly accurate. It is nothing but a compilation by a potentially biased party and we urge the Chamber not to consider it, not to allow it to be used or to admit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic, do you wish to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, with great pleasure. Mr. President, I have presented an original document on the convicting of -- among others, Jusufagic Said who was mentioned, and the witness has spoken about him. That is the first point. On the other hand, the Prosecution presented a photocopy of a document which was not even signed whereas I am presenting an original document. I would like to have this document introduced into evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Deretic, let me ask you a question. What is the relevance of the criminal record of possible victims of beatings in the camp? I just want to hear your theory of the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Madam Judge Wald, through my questions, I merely wished to substantiate the statement made by the witness. He said that he did know these people personally and that in the meantime, before everything happened in Keraterm, they were people that were convicted. They were criminals and were convicted on several occasions and did have a criminal record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But if I may pursue that, why would that be relevant to beating, to whether or not they were victims of beating in the camp? I thought possibly you might be getting at the notion that that might show who was likely to have beat them because they had been criminals, but if it just goes to the notion that they were "bad people," I would agree with the Prosecution, that wouldn't be relevant. How bad you were doesn't mean that people can beat you up at will. So I'm just trying to figure out what you think the relevance of their criminal record is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Wald. Quite so. My main reason was to show that the people who were charged criminally led and took part, first and foremost, in the attack on Prijedor, and that as such, they were highly noticeable people, conspicuous. And it was these people, for the most part, who were beaten in Keraterm, those with criminal records, who had taken part in the attack, not because of ethnic affiliation but because they put up active resistance to the take-over of power and everything that took place in Prijedor during that time, from the takeover of power to the attack on Prijedor. They were prominent in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see Ms. Susan Somers on her feet. We can't prolong the debate. Do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm waiting for a ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Mr. Deretic, have you completed your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. No. I'm just halfway there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand why you're asking the -- why you're tendering the document for admission now. Why not wait until the end? That's why I asked you whether you had finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the last time that I questioned a witness, I asked -- I tendered documents towards the end, but the Chamber put off ruling, and I thought that this was an opportune moment to reintroduce that and to tender the document, whether the Chamber accepts or rejects at the time when you ask, request, at the pertinent moment in conformity with the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic, for me to be able to find my way, the end goal of this document is to show that these people merited what they got because they were bad citizens, bad subjects. So they deserved what they got. Is that what you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I never for a moment thought that nor do I mean it now. I just wish to document and substantiate the fact that through force of circumstance in these particular cases, they were people who were active participants in the attack on Prijedor. I didn't say that they deserved to be beaten and that they were punished for that. There were other people of different ethnic groups who unfortunately suffered the same fate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we are going to take a break, to adjourn, to calm down, and I don't like having this kind of discussion in the presence of the witness. The witness is here with us. So I would prefer to have a discussion of this kind at the end. But let us adjourn for half an hour, and we will come back with a ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Very well. Mr. Deretic, we shall now continue with the examination of the witness. We shall now continue with the direct examination of the witness. Yes, please proceed. And we shall give our ruling at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness DD/9, during your stay in Keraterm, did you hear of a person called Fajzo Mujkanovic?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know when was that person brought to the investigation centre?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know if there were any conflicts, any problems relative to that person?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: No [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's answer was yes. The interpreter excuses herself.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So what was the conflict about?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Well, Duca Knezevic came once inquiring about his brother who was under age and who had been killed by Muslims. I do not know exactly where whether it was Kozarac or Kozarusa or somewhere, I'm not sure. And I know that Duca came to ask him about his brother.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know where did this Mujkanovic come from?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: From the area of Kozarac, but I don't know what part exactly. Kozarusa, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know, after Dusko Knezevic asked this man about his minor brother, do you know what happened then?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: You mean to that person, Fajzo Mujkanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: I do not know exactly what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did Dusko Knezevic hit him on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Perhaps he did once or twice.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Leading, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Leading and an indication of he did not know what happened to him. Counsel is testifying for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic, will you rephrase your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I cannot rephrase this question nor is it a leading question. I'm asking the witness whether he knows if Dusko Knezevic hit the witness, that is, the person who had been brought in. I don't know why it's leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Perhaps -- I see in the transcript a question -- no, it is an answer. The witness said -- this is not a question. This is affirmation. But if you ask if Knezevic beat him on that occasion, there is nothing leading there. So please proceed. Ms. Susan Somers, what was the question? What is leading in this question, I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The objection, Your Honour, was on page 41, line 8. The response to, "Do you know what happened to that person?" was, "I do not know exactly what happened to him," and then counsel suggested about a beating and he suddenly knew what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, when I asked, the witness evidently gave a completely different answer. He said he did not know what happened to the man in the end, and my question has to do with whether Dusan Knezevic hit him, did the witness see Dusan Knezevic hit Fejzo Mujkanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, proceed. Proceed. Because Ms. Susan Somers, I do not know exactly what happened to him exactly. So one can still ask a general question and in general terms. "Exactly," that does not answer that question. At least that is my opinion, but we can really not go on discussing all these matters. Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So once again, Witness, did you see whether after his question, Duca Knezevic hit Fejzo Mujkanovic?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did he curse him?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know or did you see Zoran Zigic ever strike that man?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: During your stay in Keraterm, do you know what happened to Fejzo Mujkanovic?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know if he's still alive today?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: I do not have any exact information. I cannot answer that question. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness DD/9, do you know if during your stay at the Keraterm Investigation Centre Room 3 had come into existence?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know a person Jasmin Ramadanovic, called Sengin, in Keraterm? Do you know that individual?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know, from your days in Keraterm, a person called Jasmin Ramadanovic, nicknamed Sengin?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Oh, Jasmin Ramadanovic, nicknamed Sengin. Yes, I know that person.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was he a man from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What did he do in Prijedor? What was his trade?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: He was in hostelry, the restaurant business.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know why he was brought to Keraterm Investigation Centre?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: From what I learned, he lived -- he lived in the old town, and from -- and a part of the attack on Prijedor came from there. They passed by his house, the men who -- according to what I know, those men who took part in the attack on Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And do you know if this man was beaten in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And during your stay in Keraterm, did you know that medical aid was extended to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. I have to interrupt you. You asked him, "Do you know if this man was beaten in Keraterm?" The answer was, "No." But you asked two questions at the same time, and we do not know whether two -- which did the witness answer "No." Is it did he know that a man was beaten? It is two questions, and when the witness says, "No," we do not know to which part of the questions he's answering. So will you rephrase the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Witness, do you know if Sengin was beaten in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know if medical aid was extended to him in the Prijedor general hospital?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: I heard about it, that he was there in the general hospital. I do not have any personal knowledge that he was beaten.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And do you know if he returned from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that, too, but I was not there.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you ever see Zoran Zigic beat that man?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: No, I did not see him beat Sengin.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And do you know what eventually happened to Sengin?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you know somebody called Drago Tokmadzic?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: I knew him by sight.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know what was he before the war in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: He was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you see him in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deretic, I believe there is too much interference and it is very difficult for the interpreters. Can the technical booth do something to reduce this? I think that the interpreters are getting too much noise and it is becoming very difficult for them to interpret, to hear the voices and interpret with all this interference. Can we get some good news, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The AV section has informed me it will take approximately a minute to correct the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not know whether the witnesses [as interpreted] can work with this. Yes. Let us try to move on. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DERETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. We could not hear the beginning. You said that you were in Keraterm together with Zoran Zigic.

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Could you tell us when was that?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: It was roughly between the 13th and the 15th July, perhaps the 14th. I'm not really sure.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And after you left it, did you continue to socialise and see one another?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: We would see the -- we would meet about the town, and there were not very many coffee shops and places like that open so that we bumped into one another there.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know after Zoran Zigic lost his job there, that he went to -- that he was in the Prijedor hospital?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
utterances.text: Yes. I know that, because the wound he had sustained, there was some complications so that he spent some time in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you tell us when was that?

utterances.speaker: Witness DD/9
